combo-no-flag-vessel.essay:
Suppose a boat or a floating home goes out onto the open ocean and flies no country's flag, or flies one its owners designed themselves. This idea combines two things, the high seas, which no country owns, and a refusal of the registration that every ordinary ship carries. People who try it often reason that with no flag there is no law. The real position is narrower than that, and one part of it is still argued over.

Start with what is clearly settled. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) is the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Under Article 92 a ship on the high seas normally answers only to the country whose flag it flies, so a foreign warship may not simply come aboard. Article 110 lists the exceptions, and one is reasonable ground for suspecting that "the ship is without nationality". The warship may then send a boat under an officer to check the papers. If suspicion remains it may search further, and if the suspicion proves unfounded the ship must be compensated. This is called the right of visit. A ship that uses two or more flags as it suits may be treated as having none (Article 92(2)). Nobody seriously disputes the boarding power, so an unflagged vessel has no treaty protection from a stop and search. Calling this a gap in the law would be wrong, because Article 110 addresses it by name.

Older rulings say more. In 1946 a British destroyer stopped the Asya about 100 miles off Jaffa. She raised a Turkish flag, then hauled it down and raised a Zionist flag, which belonged to no state. In Molvan v Attorney General for Palestine (1948) the Privy Council, then the top court for the British Empire, said freedom of the open sea belongs to ships that fly and are entitled to fly the flag of a state, and that the Asya "could not claim the protection of any State". In United States v. Marino-Garcia (1982) a US appeals court upheld drug convictions of nine foreign crewmen on the Four Roses, stopped about 65 miles off Cuba with nothing linking the cargo to the United States. The court called stateless vessels "international pariahs" and required no connection to the United States.

The open question is what may follow the boarding. Article 110 speaks only of verifying and examining. By contrast, Article 105 lets any state seize a pirate ship and try those aboard, and Article 109 allows arrest for illegal broadcasting. No such words appear for a ship without nationality. So writers divide. The "any state" view holds that any country may apply its law to a stateless vessel, and Churchill and Lowe are cited for a broad power to intervene. The "nexus" view requires some link, such as the crew's nationality, and Bennett is cited for limiting a boarding state to inspection. In 2025 Andrew Norris argued that states have been needlessly timid and may assert full jurisdiction. In 2026 Thea Coventry of Leiden argued that boarding does not by itself give power over foreigners' conduct, and that "sailing a vessel without nationality is not itself an international crime". The Enrica Lexie tribunal accepted that states may exceptionally use high-seas freedoms through small non-registered vessels, which shows that being unregistered does not in every case mean being outside the law's protection. No international court has decided the point.

National courts have mostly gone one way, under their own statutes. The United States defines a "vessel without nationality" in the Maritime Drug Law Enforcement Act (46 USC 70502), including a vessel whose named country denies the registry. In 2008 the Drug Trafficking Vessel Interdiction Act (18 USC 2285) made it a crime to operate an unflagged submersible beyond a territorial sea with intent to evade detection. In United States v. Aybar-Ulloa in 2021 the First Circuit, a US appeals court, held that international law permits prosecuting foreigners seized on a stateless vessel. A panel of the same court ruled in 2022 that one part of the definition went beyond what Congress could do, and the full court in 2023 cancelled that ruling on narrower grounds without deciding the question. The Eleventh Circuit said in 2025 that the US definition is not limited by customary international law. Other countries are moving too. Britain boarded the tanker Smyrtos on 14 June 2026, and its defence ministry said that once a vessel is found stateless Britain can use its domestic powers. Early accounts placed the boarding on the high seas and later ones said the ship had entered British waters, so the case may not test the high-seas question. A group of Nordic and Baltic states said in 2025 that vessels with no flag have no right to freedom of navigation. These are national positions, and other states have not all accepted them.

Follow what would happen to a harmless stateless habitat. If no warship cares, nothing happens at first. Then the indirect routes begin. Each person aboard remains a national of some country, which can reach them. The United States claims power over certain crimes by or against its nationals in places outside any nation's jurisdiction (18 USC 7(7)) and taxes citizens abroad under Cook v. Tait. Ports ask for the ship's papers. Insurance cover usually lapses when a ship loses its flag, according to the group Human Rights at Sea, and radio licences, safety inspections and crew documents normally come through a flag state. The tanker Sea Princess was struck off the Cook Islands register while at sea on its way to scrap, and its crew were left with no flag state responsible for sending them home. If a stateless vessel is robbed or rammed, no government is obliged to speak for it.

Reading the text, it seems that being stateless is not itself an offence under UNCLOS, and that a country needs its own law and some accepted ground before it can punish anyone aboard. The potential lies there, and it is small. The strongest version is a small vessel doing nothing else that any state prohibits, attracting no attention, with occupants who accept that they have no protection. It holds only as long as nobody chooses to act. Announcing a new country is what draws attention, as the XLII seastead off Phuket found in 2019 when Thailand charged its occupants, and that was a structure inside a coastal zone.

combo-company-run-flag.essay:
Many people are surprised to learn that some national ship registers are run by private companies, sometimes on another continent. A ship flying the flag of Liberia is registered through a company based in Virginia. That raises an obvious thought for a founder. If a flag is a service sold by a company, perhaps a founder could negotiate with that company, or set up one like it for a small country, and obtain a flag on special terms. The idea combines an ordinary flag, a deal with a host government and a business arrangement.

The history explains how this came about. Liberia's register began in 1948 under President William Tubman with the help of Edward Stettinius, a former US Secretary of State, and the first ship, the World Peace, was registered in March 1949. The International Trust Company ran it until 1999, when Liberia's government appointed the Liberian International Ship and Corporate Registry (LISCR), a Delaware company based in Virginia, to manage the register and collect the fees owed to the state. That appointment rests on an Act of the Liberian Legislature. The register brings in roughly $24 million a year, and in the 2007-08 budget it was about six percent of government revenue, while during the civil war maritime money was about 70 percent. International Registries, Inc. of Reston, Virginia, descends from the original Stettinius company. According to one account it moved its business to the Marshall Islands after Charles Taylor demanded too much money. The timing of that move is not clear, since the Marshall Islands government started its register in 1988 and Taylor's government gave the Liberian contract to LISCR in 1999. International Registries provides its administrative and technical support, including vessel registration, inspections, seafarer documents and radio licences.

The law on who holds the power is clear. Article 91 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, says "every State" fixes the conditions for its nationality and that ships have the nationality of the state whose flag they may fly. A company can process the paperwork and collect fees, but the nationality comes from the state. Article 94 places the duties of supervision on the state as well. Open registers are generally accepted as lawful, and the writer Eduardo Cavalcanti de Mello Filho treats that as settled, while noting that a small state can be a responsible flag. The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea held in the M/V Saiga (No. 2) case that the genuine link requirement in Article 91 gives other countries no criteria for challenging a ship's registration.

Some things are open. Whether a third state may refuse to respect a flag whose government knowingly lets ships evade supervision is unsettled. Mello Filho calls these "flags of deceit", and he argues that the Saiga reasoning is thin and that non-recognition may be available. The Tribunal's approach suggests the only remedy is to report the problem to the flag state under Article 94(6). So a registry that exists mainly to sell cover may stay valid on paper while other governments test how far they can ignore it.

Recent events show how far a state can hand this work over and what can then go wrong. Gabon authorised a UAE-based firm, Intershipping Services, to run its register in 2018. By 2024 it was the fastest-growing by tonnage, and the EU and Britain sanctioned the firm in July 2025. Comoros withdrew authority from private operators and brought certificate issuance back in house. Cameroon expelled the tanker Smyrtos from its register in May 2026, and Britain boarded it the next month. Earlier, Sweden pressed Nicaragua to withdraw the registration of the Radio Nord ship, and the owners moved it to Panama's register. In each case the state's decision was the one that counted.

Follow a founder through this. The ordinary route is available. A company formed for the purpose applies, the ship passes vetting on age, condition and owner, the owners are screened against sanctions lists, and the fee is paid. The result is a normal flag with that country's law on board and no special status. Reading the text, it seems nothing in Article 91 would prevent a small state from writing a statute that offers a special class of register for residential platforms, or appointing a founder's company as its registrar, as Liberia and Gabon appointed theirs. That would need a government and a legislature willing to act, and the registry company itself could not offer it. It would also bring the founder's company under the law of wherever it is based. Companies in Virginia answer to American courts and sanctions rules, and Liberia's statute limits LISCR's investors to US nationals.

The deal would be weak in the ways that matter most to a founder. A government that grants a registry contract can end it, as Liberia did in 1999, and a change of president could change the terms. Pressure from a powerful state tends to arrive at a small government's door. MS Satoshi's owners asked Panama to class their ship as non-seagoing, which would have lifted most treaty duties, and Panama refused. The flag would also carry its treaty obligations on safety and crew, since a state cannot contract those away by private agreement. A special class that left a ship with no real supervision would risk being treated as a flag of deceit.

The strongest version is a small state that passes a real law, supervises real safety standards, and contracts a founder's company to do the administration in return for fees that matter to its budget. No founder is known to have done this. Liberia shows that the money can matter a great deal to a state's budget, which gives a government a reason to agree, and it also shows that governments sometimes squeeze a registry for revenue. It would give stability and a say over the paperwork. Sovereignty would remain with the state that owns the flag.

combo-always-moving-habitat.essay:
This idea avoids building anything fixed. A community lives on a ship that never stays long in one place, sailing across open ocean, passing through countries' coastal waters and calling at one port after another. It combines a flagged ship with the rule that lets ships pass through a country's waters, called innocent passage. The hope is that a home in constant motion never settles under any coastal government for long enough to be governed by it.

Much of this is settled and in the founder's favour. A ship under a real flag is lawful, and Article 90 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, gives every state the right to sail ships on the high seas. There, under Article 92, the ship answers only to its flag state. No treaty limits how long a ship may keep sailing. A moving ship also avoids the main rule that stops platforms. Article 60 gives a coastal state control over artificial islands and structures in its 200-mile resource zone, and a ship passing through is not one of these. Article 58 keeps the freedom of navigation in that zone for all countries. MS The World has worked this way since 2002, with residents who own their apartments and elect an advisory board, under the Bahamian flag.

The rules become tighter near a coast. The territorial sea is the belt up to 12 nautical miles from shore, where a country has full authority apart from the right of innocent passage (Article 17). Passage has a specific meaning. Article 18 says it means sailing through without entering port, or going to or from a port, and that it "shall be continuous and expeditious". Stopping and anchoring count only when they are a normal part of navigation or forced by distress. Article 19 lists what makes passage not innocent, including loading or unloading any person or goods contrary to customs or immigration laws, research, launching aircraft, and "any other activity not having a direct bearing on passage". So innocent passage is a right to cross. It is no basis for lingering, and it gives no right to live offshore in one spot within 12 miles.

Ports are the part most often misunderstood. A flag gives no right to enter a port. Ports lie in internal waters, and Article 25(2) recognises that a coastal state may set conditions on admission and act to prevent any breach of them. Women on Waves, whose Dutch-flagged ship carries a clinic, found this in 2004 when Portuguese warships blocked it. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2009 that Portugal had breached freedom of expression, but that ruling rested on human rights law. In Guatemala the army blocked the pier within 24 hours of the ship docking. Once in port, residents and the ship fall under that country's law as well.

Some points are open. Women on Waves also raises the unresolved question of whether a ship that docks, boards a country's citizens and takes them out for an act banned at home is passing innocently. Whether a ship used as a permanent home, returning to the same waters again and again, stays within the words "continuous and expeditious" has not been tested in any known ruling. Reading the text, it seems that the passage rules look at what the ship is doing on each trip through the belt, and that a home on a real route would be treated like any passenger ship. A ship that repeatedly drifted just offshore for residents' convenience would look more like the stopping that Article 18 does not allow. A practical point follows from this. A ship registered as seagoing has to keep the certificates and crew that go with that, and a resident community may struggle to pay for them.

Follow one year of such a life. The flag state's law applies on board. Crew and safety rules follow the flag, under Article 94. Every landing is an immigration event. A resident has to hold a passport and any visa that each port demands, so a person without valid papers stays on board or is refused. Food, fuel and spare parts come from ports, and repairs from shipyards. The move-along approach gives no escape from tax, because a citizen's home country may tax regardless of where the person sleeps, as the United States does under Cook v. Tait. Banks ask for a home address and a tax residence. Medical care beyond the ship's clinic means going ashore. A child born on board usually takes nationality from the parents, and the 1961 statelessness treaty treats the birth as occurring in the flag country only to prevent statelessness.

The cases show that the money usually fails before the law does. Villa Vie Odyssey sold cabins from $99,999, and on 26 October 2026 in Sihanoukville residents were told to leave because the company could not secure fuel. Life at Sea Cruises cancelled its three-year voyage in 2023 without ever having a ship. MS Satoshi failed for a different reason, because it was meant to stay at anchor, and liability insurers would not cover a ship used that way. That suggests that continual sailing can be easier to insure than sitting still, though the cost of fuel and crew is far higher.

This route has more practical potential than nearly any other at sea, and it achieves less in sovereignty. The strongest version is a solid company or residents' association owning a well-maintained ship under a respected flag, on a real itinerary, with a private contract setting the internal rules. Such a community can last for decades and choose where it goes. Its members stay citizens of their own countries, its flag state can remove it from the register, and any port can refuse it. Having no territory also leaves it without a basis for statehood under the usual tests.

add_sources.t: Villa Vie Odyssey Residents Ordered Off Ship as Fuel Crisis Forces Layup, Cruise Hive, Oct 2026
Villa Vie set to file Chapter 11 after Odyssey residents left in Cambodia, Cruise Industry News, 29 Oct 2026

combo-low-tide-with-claimant.essay:
In disputed seas such as the South China Sea, several countries claim the same reefs. A private founder could not hold such a place alone, since rival navies are close by. The idea here is to approach one of the claimants and offer to develop a reef that dries at low tide, in return for a charter or a concession. The claimant gets a presence that supports its position, and the founder gets a protector. This combines reef law, a territorial dispute and a host government's grant.

Start with what the law says about the reef. A low-tide elevation is natural land that is above water at low tide and under water at high tide (UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, Article 13). The International Court of Justice said in Qatar v Bahrain in 2001 that treaty law is silent on whether such features can be considered territory, and that state practice does not clearly allow or exclude taking them. In 2008, in the Pedra Branca case between Malaysia and Singapore, it held that sovereignty over South Ledge, a low-tide elevation, "belongs to the State in whose territorial waters it lies". In the South China Sea arbitration, decided in 2016, the Philippines asked the panel to find that Mischief Reef, Second Thomas Shoal and Subi Reef are low-tide elevations and "not features that are capable of appropriation by occupation or otherwise". The panel agreed that all three were submerged at high tide in their natural condition, and it said that a feature is judged by its natural state before any building. Its reasoning keeps treating Mischief Reef as a low-tide elevation for the purpose of appropriation even after China built on it. China took no part and rejects the award, and an award binds only the parties, so its reach as a rule is argued over, though its reasoning is widely cited. Filling in a reef makes an artificial island, which has no territorial sea (Article 60(8)).

Robert Beckman of the National University of Singapore summarises the working position. A low-tide elevation within a territorial sea comes under the coastal state's sovereignty through its rights over the seabed. One beyond the territorial sea is part of the shelf, where the coastal state has rights over resources. In overlapping zones no state can claim sovereignty over such a feature, and which state holds the rights must wait for a boundary agreement. In the meantime states should make provisional arrangements and avoid unilateral acts.

So the founder's partner may not own what it is offering. The open question is what a permit from one claimant is worth while the zone is undelimited. Article 60 says the coastal state alone may authorise artificial islands in its zone. Reading the text, it seems that the permit is good if that claimant proves to be the coastal state and worthless, or a wrongful act, if it does not, and that nobody can say which until a boundary is agreed. The other claimants would treat the work as a violation at once. How a tribunal would treat a private investor who relied on one claimant's permit has not been tested in this setting.

A real example of a partnership of this kind is Layang-Layang, or Swallow Reef, in the Spratly Islands. Malaysian special forces put up a plaque in 1980 and built an encampment in 1983. Malaysia reclaimed land, raising the area from 6.2 to 35 hectares, and built a runway of 1,367 metres and a navy station. A dive resort operated there under Malaysian licence. China, Taiwan and Vietnam also claim the reef. On 6 January 2025 Malaysia revoked the resort's operating licence and it closed. The investor's position rested on one government's decision, and that government changed it. The example shows the business pattern. It says nothing about the reef's status in law, which would depend on its natural state before reclamation.

Tomás Cloma's Freedomland shows the private version of the idea going badly. He claimed part of the Spratlys in 1956 and asked the Philippine government for support. Taiwan's navy burned buildings there, and in 1974 the Philippines arrested him and made him sign over his rights. The partner he had courted took what he had claimed. The Minerva group in the South Pacific sought no partner, and Tonga annexed the reef in 1972.

Follow how the partnership would work. The claimant's law would apply, because that is the only source of the charter. Its navy decides who may land, and it may want the site for a garrison. Banks and insurers look at sanctions risk and war risk, and they would have to consider that a rival claimant regards the project as illegal. Other governments may warn their nationals off, since a home country's laws can reach its citizens. Workers need visas from the claimant, and their goods come through its ports. If shooting starts, the founder has no standing to negotiate. Under the South China Sea award's reasoning, a rival could later argue that the project sits on its seabed and demand its removal.

The potential is real but narrow. A founder could gain a physical base, a garrison next door and a commercial licence, as the Layang-Layang resort had until 2025. The strongest version would be a place where two claimants agree to joint development, so that the permit comes from both and the dispute is set aside, along the lines Beckman describes as a provisional arrangement. The Mauritius and Seychelles joint shelf is a peaceful model of two states sharing a seabed, though it is not a dispute over a reef. Independence is not on offer in any version, because the only thing that protects the project is a state's claim, and that state's interest is in strengthening its own position.

add_sources.t: The South China Sea Award, Artificial Islands and Territory, Australian Year Book of International Law

combo-buy-grandfathered-structure.essay:
A new founder might reason that Sealand has already done the hard part. It has been occupied since 1967, Britain has left it alone, and its family has issued coins and titles for decades. Perhaps the shortest route is to buy it or a structure like it, or to inherit one, and so step into a position nobody could build today. This idea combines an old platform with a purchase. The question is what a sale can actually transfer.

The law separates two things. One is ownership or possession of a structure, which a private person can have. The other is the authority to govern a place, which only states have and which is not sold with the structure. In the case of Sealand, the fort stood outside Britain's three-mile territorial sea when Roy Bates took it. In October 1968 a judge at Chelmsford held that a firearms law did not apply there, because Parliament had not extended it that far. James Grimmelmann, in his detailed legal history of Sealand, explains that the ruling is much narrower than the family claims. It says Parliament had not legislated for the fort, and it does not say Parliament could not. In 1978 a court in Cologne held that Sealand was no state, and no country has recognised it. On 1 October 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which covers the tower. UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, allows that breadth (Article 3), and Grimmelmann writes that the extension reached far enough to take in the fort. Sealand claims a share of those waters, and he concludes that international law favours Britain on that. All of that was fixed before any buyer arrives, so a buyer would inherit a fort inside British waters.

The rest is less clear. Who holds title to the fort is itself uncertain. Accounts differ on when Britain left. Grimmelmann says the Maunsell forts were abandoned in 1948, and another account says the last full-time staff left Roughs Tower in 1956. Bates took it by occupation. Government lawyers concluded in the 1960s that a civil action to recover it would probably fail, and officials working to a Ministry of Defence plan offered him £5,000 to leave. A buyer would be purchasing possession and a contested history, and there is no land register that could prove a good title. Whether a British court would give effect to a sale or a will of the fort has not been tested. The family's mailing address runs through a British postbag. When Roy Bates died in 2012 his son Michael took over without any government stepping in, and he lives in England. Reading the facts, it seems that the inheritance worked because it changed nothing that Britain cared about, and that this is no sign that Britain accepted it as a succession to a throne.

The other uncertain matter is why Britain leaves the fort alone, because the tolerance is the real asset. A Cabinet Office meeting in November 1968 concluded that Bates was doing no actual harm and that force or special legislation was not justified. British policy since then has treated Sealand as a non-state. It has not removed the occupants since 1987. Tolerance of this kind was given to a particular family with a modest footprint, and a sale would change who it was being given to. Reading the facts, it seems that a buyer whose purpose was to host material or activity banned elsewhere would be asking the same government for a different decision.

Real attempts show this. In January 2007 The Pirate Bay, a file-sharing index, tried to buy Sealand as a base after copyright pressure in Sweden. Between 2007 and 2010 Sealand was offered through a Spanish estate company, InmoNaranja, at an asking price of €750 million. No sale took place. Earlier, Alexander Achenbach invited the elder Bateses to Austria in 1978 to discuss a sale, and his associates seized the fort while they were away. The family retook it by helicopter. HavenCo, a data-hosting firm, was a tenant rather than a buyer, and it shows the risks of depending on the family. It promised customers protection from courts, it had about ten customers, and in 2002 the family took over the company and its servers.

Follow what a real sale would involve. The buyer pays money through a bank, which asks what is being purchased and from whom. The answer is a structure in British territorial waters, and tax and money-laundering questions follow in Britain and in the buyer's own country. A lender has no security. Insurers look at a wartime concrete fort that burned in 2006, and an RAF helicopter took the person aboard to hospital then, because Britain is the nearest authority. The buyer's staff need boats from British ports. If the buyer sold passports, the 1997 passport scandal shows what follows. Other old structures offer less. Most sea forts and platforms stand on someone's shelf or inside waters that have since been extended, and Article 60 requires disused installations in a coastal zone to be removed for safety. A disused platform that was never occupied has no such history behind it.

The potential is modest but real, and it is mainly a matter of name and history. A buyer gains a famous brand, a place people have heard of, a physical site and a very long record of being left alone. The strongest version would be a purchase from the family with continuity of the same low-key use, where no one is harmed in Britain and nobody tests the arrangement. That could continue for years. It would add nothing in law, because no title to govern was ever available from the seller.

combo-drifting-ice-no-flag.essay:
The idea here is to live on a large piece of drifting ice in open ocean, with no ship and no flag. This combines floating ice with the high seas, and it has a particular appeal in law. An iceberg is not obviously a ship, so the flag rules might not apply. It is not obviously land either, so the rules against claiming land might not apply, and it moves about on water that no state owns.

Very little here is settled. UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, does not mention icebergs apart from a clause on ice-covered areas of a coastal state's zone. Its general rules still give some footing. Article 89 bars any state from claiming part of the high seas. Article 121 defines an island as "a naturally formed area of land", which reading the text does not appear to fit floating ice. Article 92 and Article 110, on flags and boarding, are written for ships. Whoever stands on the ice remains a national of some country, and nothing about ice changes that. Inside a coastal state's zone the position is different. Matthew Paterson, writing in 2019, suggests that a coastal state's rights over natural resources in its 200-mile zone cover icebergs, and Canada requires licences to harvest them in its waters.

What the ice itself is in law is open, and writers disagree. Mateusz Osiecki, writing in 2022, sets out three views of a free-floating iceberg. One calls it res nullius, belonging to no one and open to the first taker, in the way a fish is. Another says it may be held under a state's claim. A third calls it res communis, shared by all like the open sea. He argues that it is no country's property and sits on the high seas. That is one writer's reasoning, and no court has ruled on it. Even if a person may take a berg as property, as Osiecki's reasoning allows, property in a block of ice is a different thing from authority to govern people on it.

The one court to come near the question did so after a killing. T-3, or Fletcher's Ice Island, was a drifting block about 11 by 5 kilometres, used as an American research station. On 16 July 1970 Mario Escamilla shot and killed the station manager there. The island lay in the sector Canada claimed, and Canada waived any jurisdiction it might have had, while saying this did not affect its claims. American officials flew him to Virginia and charged him under the law for crimes at sea, and in United States v. Escamilla (1972) the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, split evenly on whether that law reached an unclaimed ice island, so the trial court's ruling on that point stayed in place. The same court overturned his conviction because of errors at trial, and he was acquitted at the retrial. Congress settled the point for American law with a change in 1984. Both men were American and the suspect was taken home by his own government. So the case shows that a person on the ice does not fall outside all law, and it leaves the status of the ice itself unsettled.

Reading the text, it seems that a person on free-floating ice with no ship could say that no warship has the Article 110 right to board, because there is no ship. The reply is the same one that applies to fixed platforms. The rule that forbids boarding other than in listed cases also protects only ships. An unflagged camp on ice would have no flag state's exclusive authority behind it, and so no state would have standing to complain if another state's officers landed. No one has tested this. In practice the nearest state would be the one that supplies the camp, and it would not need to land to stop it.

Follow what would actually happen. The first need is an aircraft or a ship, which has a flag and a base in some country. Camp Barneo near the North Pole shows the pattern. It was a private camp, rebuilt from nothing each April, and every trip from 2002 to 2017 ran through Longyearbyen on Svalbard. When Chechen paratroopers exercised at Barneo in 2016 Norway imposed a flight ban. A dispute between Russia and Ukraine stopped tourist flights in 2019. The camp last operated in 2018, and no one had to board the ice to end it. Soviet and Russian drift stations show that people can live on floes for years, as North Pole-22 did for nine, with a government supplying them, and from the mid-2000s safe floes were hard to find. Antarctic ice has its own dangers, since A23a, once the largest iceberg in the world at about 3,500 square kilometres, was gone or nearly so by July 2026 after leaving cold water. Max Perutz warned in 1942 that bergs can roll over.

The money problems come next. A berg cannot be mortgaged in any meaningful way, as it may not exist in a few years, and no registry lists it. Liability insurers would have nothing to rate. Radio equipment needs licences from a state. Residents' home countries still tax and prosecute them, as Escamilla's case shows. A rescue depends on the nearest government's goodwill, and it ends in that government's territory. If the ice drifts into a coastal zone, as A23a did when it grounded 73 kilometres from South Georgia, a coastal state's rights come into play with no action by the residents.

The potential is limited, and it lies in the real legal uncertainty. The strongest version is a large, stable tabular berg in cold water, occupied by a small group with an aircraft or ship under a real flag, claiming property in the ice at most and no sovereignty. That would be a temporary station, lasting a season to a few years, with the supply ship's flag state as the practical authority. Declaring a state on it would add no rights.

combo-submersible-beyond-waters.essay:
A submarine is hard to see. Some people imagine a community living in a large submersible that stays below the surface in open ocean, moving from place to place, unseen and so effectively outside government. This combines undersea living, the high seas and the question of flags. It helps to separate what the law says from what hiding can achieve, because they are different questions.

The law on the water is fairly plain. Depth creates no separate legal zone. The water column beyond national limits follows the high-seas rules, and under Article 87 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, all states may navigate there. Article 20 requires submarines and other underwater vehicles in a territorial sea, the belt up to 12 nautical miles from a coast, to travel on the surface and show their flag. No similar rule applies further out, so a submerged vessel on the high seas under a real flag is allowed, and its flag state's law applies aboard. UNCLOS does not define "ship", so treating a submersible as one is an inference, though the Canadian safety board noted in its report on the Titan that submersibles fall within the definition of a vessel in Canadian law. Article 110, which lets a warship board a ship suspected of having no nationality, would seem to apply to a submersible, once a warship has found it and it has surfaced or been stopped.

The United States has gone further for one kind of vessel. The Drug Trafficking Vessel Interdiction Act of 2008 (18 USC 2285) makes it a crime to operate or embark on a submersible or semi-submersible that has no nationality, beyond any country's territorial sea, "with the intent to evade detection". The penalty is up to 15 years in prison, and the law expressly applies abroad. A person charged has a defence if the vessel was lawfully registered, built to a classification society's rules, engaged in licensed commerce, research or exploration, or running a working tracking system. Congress's stated concern was drug trafficking and terrorism, but the words do not require drugs to be found. American appeals courts have upheld it. In United States v. Saac and United States v. Ibarguen-Mosquera the Eleventh Circuit rejected challenges to Congress's power, and in Valarezo-Orobio in 2011 it applied those rulings to a 35-foot semi-submersible that its crew scuttled near Malpelo Island. Whether other countries accept that this law may bind their citizens on the high seas when no link to the United States exists falls within the wider dispute about stateless vessels. That dispute is unresolved in international law, and the US cases rest on US constitutional law.

Reading the text, it seems that this statute reaches close to the idea discussed here. A long-stay unflagged submersible, built to avoid notice, is close to what Congress described, even if nobody aboard has done anything else. It would apply wherever American officers can reach the people concerned, including when they next come ashore in a country that cooperates. A registered and tracked submersible falls outside the statute, and it also gives up the advantage of being hidden.

The Titan shows how little a flag can matter until something goes wrong, and how much is then asked. OceanGate's Titan was not registered in any country and not classed or certified by anyone. OceanGate began registering an earlier hull in the Bahamas in 2019 and did not pursue it after learning the requirements. The dive site at the Titanic wreck lies beyond Canada's 200-mile zone. The support ship, Polar Prince, flew Canada's flag. After the fatal implosion in June 2023, investigators from Canada and the United States took up the case, and in 2026 the Canadian board recommended that Canada require submersibles operating with a Canadian support ship to meet safety guidance and that the guidance be made binding internationally. So an unregistered craft operated in open ocean for years with no regulator. Investigators could still reach the company and its support ship, because both had known addresses and countries.

Follow what long-term life would involve. Private submersibles today make dives lasting hours. Long-endurance submarines belong to navies, and the parts for them are tightly controlled exports. Any battery or diesel craft has to surface or reach a supply point often. Food, spare parts and crew changes come from ports or from a surface ship that has a flag and a registered owner. Radio use from under water is limited, and using radio at the surface needs a licence from a state. Medical emergencies mean surfacing and asking for help, and a rescue under Article 98 ends in a coastal state. A child born aboard would depend on the parents' nationality. Article 20 means any approach to a coast has to be made on the surface under a flag, and a coastal state may treat an unknown submarine in its waters as a security matter.

The potential is narrow. Hiding works for a while, and it gives no legal status. A hidden community has no way to bank, insure, trade openly or be recognised, because all of those depend on being known. The strongest version is the reverse of hiding, a registered and classed submersible or small fleet under a real flag, operating publicly from a registered support ship. Such a craft can stay on the high seas under its flag state's law, and residents could spend long periods below. It would be under that state's law and easy to find.

combo-platform-with-sinking-state.essay:
Several low-lying Pacific countries expect rising seas to make their land hard to live on. They are real states with UN seats, large sea zones and few resources for adaptation. A founder might propose a partnership. The founder would finance floating or raised platforms in the state's own sea zone, and the state would grant a charter and its legal cover. If the land one day disappears, the platforms might be part of how the state continues. This combines a coastal zone, a host's grant and the idea of a state without ordinary territory. It has never been done.

The sea-zone part is settled. Article 60 of UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, gives a coastal state the exclusive right to authorise artificial islands in its exclusive economic zone, and sole legal power over them. So a small island state could lawfully permit a platform in its own waters. Article 60(8) also says such a platform is not an island and has no territorial sea of its own. In 2011 Kiribati's president Anote Tong mentioned floating islands, comparing them to oil rigs, at a cost of about $2 billion, and his government went on to buy land in Fiji instead.

The question of what happens to the state is moving quickly and is not closed. The usual test for statehood, in the 1933 Montevideo Convention, includes a defined territory. Pacific states have argued that a state continues even if its land is fully inundated, and that its zones continue. The Pacific Islands Forum issued a declaration on statehood in 2023. In its 2025 advisory opinion on climate change, the International Court of Justice said that loss of territory "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood", and that UNCLOS does not require states to update baselines once they are established. Judge Peter Tomka wrote separately that "territory has been indispensable to the concept of a State". On 24 September 2026 all 193 UN members adopted by consensus a political declaration that states a presumption in favour of continued statehood despite sea-level rise, and says that states may keep their maritime zones once baselines are set. Harry Aitken, an Australian diplomat who led negotiations on the declaration's legal elements and who writes in his personal capacity, describes this as a beginning, and the declaration's legal force and working details remain to be shown through what states do. Australia and Tuvalu signed the Falepili Union treaty on 9 November 2023, and it entered into force on 28 August 2024. Australia's foreign ministry says it is the first legally binding treaty to recognise that a state continues despite sea-level rise.

The reported texts do not address platforms. Reading them, it seems that continued statehood is grounded in the state's existing legal identity and in other states' agreement to keep treating it as a state. A platform would be useful for housing people and would not itself supply the missing territory, since Article 60(8) denies it island status. Whether a state whose only physical presence is a set of platforms in its own zone would be treated as the same state is an open question. The presumption in the 2026 declaration would help it. Tomka's view would count against it, and no court has decided.

Follow how the partnership might go. The first problem is consent. The declaration speaks of "mobility with dignity" and says that relocation must be voluntary. A foreign investor offering to build the future home of a nation, in exchange for a charter, is asking a small state and its voters to give up something sensitive, and the French Polynesia case shows that local opposition can end such a plan even when ministers agree. The second is money. Kiribati's figure of $2 billion came with the remark that other countries would have to pay. It appears that aid of that kind would reach the state first, so a private founder would depend on the government for it. The third is control. Article 60(2) gives the host fiscal and immigration power, and the host could revoke a charter later, as Honduras's court ended its zones in 2024. For the founder, the state's recognition is the main asset, and the founder cannot own it. The state's UN seat, passports, bank links and treaties are the state's own. The founder's residents would need to be the state's citizens or permitted foreigners, so the state's nationality law would decide who may live there. Tuvalu's own plan so far has been a digital archive of its land and culture and agreements with other countries that it stays a state, which suggests where its priorities lie.

The potential is higher than for other platform routes, in one specific sense. This is the one situation in which a platform would stand under a recognised state that has a strong reason to want it and whose continued existence other states have just promised to presume. Banks, insurers and ports would be dealing with a real government. The strongest version is led by the state itself, with outside finance on ordinary commercial or aid terms, with residents' consent, under the state's own law. What it cannot offer is a new country for the founder. The sovereignty would be that of the existing state. A founder seeking control would be asking that state to give up what it is working to keep, and the French Polynesia case suggests how local voters may respond. The recognition figure below refers to a new separate entity. The host itself already has recognition.

add_sources.t: Australia-Tuvalu Falepili Union treaty, Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

combo-unrecognised-state-in-space.essay:
An unrecognised state is a place with a real government and population whose statehood few or no countries accept, such as Somaliland or Northern Cyprus. A project might ask one of these governments to act as its launching state. The unrecognised state would authorise the launch, keep a register and take responsibility, so that the project would sit under a friendly authority that holds real land. It combines the zone of unrecognised states with orbit.

It helps to see the formal position first. The space treaties are open to "States". The UN's table of treaty members, as of 1 January 2026, has no row for Taiwan, Somaliland, Northern Cyprus or Abkhazia. Taiwan shows that the absence is more about politics than ability. It has its own government and elections, and the UN since 1971 has treated the People's Republic of China as the holder of China's seat. The Republic of China, the formal name of Taiwan's government, ratified the Outer Space Treaty in 1970, before that change. The People's Republic calls that ratification illegal, Taiwan says it will keep following the treaty, and the United States says Taiwan remains bound. North Korea shows the reverse. It is a UN member, heavily isolated, and it has joined all four main space treaties, and the UN lists an object on its register. So the ability to use the system depends on recognition by other states and the UN.

Under the Registration Convention, only a launching state, or a qualifying intergovernmental organisation, can register an object and report it to the UN Secretary-General. A self-declared state that tried to report would need the Secretary-General's office to accept it as a state, and the treaty gives it no way to insist. To be a member of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), which coordinates frequencies, a country outside the UN needs the agreement of two-thirds of members. That sets a very high bar.

The law also gives such places some standing. Statehood, under Article 3 of the Montevideo Convention of 1933, is said not to depend on recognition, and it lists four tests. Reading that together with Article VII of the Outer Space Treaty, it seems that a place meeting those tests, with a rocket leaving its soil, might be said to be a launching state in fact. If it has not joined, the treaty text does not reach it, and the parent state may be treated as the responsible party in law. The parent state's position is what other countries usually adopt. Somaliland's soil, for instance, is treated by most countries as Somalia's. Reading the text, a launch from Somaliland might be counted as a launch from Somalia's "territory", even though Somalia has no control there. The treaty itself would not hold Somalia to that, because Article VII speaks of each "State Party" and Somalia has signed the treaty without ratifying it. The English Court of Appeal's 2010 decision on flights to Northern Cyprus points the same way in air law. KTHY, which the court described as a Turkish airline, asked Britain for permission to fly to Ercan airport in the north. The trial judge found that the Republic of Cyprus has exclusive sovereignty over the airspace of the whole island, and that finding was not challenged on appeal. The Court of Appeal held that Cyprus keeps its rights under the Chicago Convention in the north, even though it lacks control there, and that granting the permit would breach the UK's duty to respect those rights. No court has applied this reasoning to a space launch, so the parallel is an inference.

What is open is what would happen in practice. No unrecognised state has launched to orbit. Other countries might hold the parent state responsible, might hold the unrecognised government responsible under general rules, or might do neither and look to the nationals and suppliers. Nothing settles how an injured country would bring a claim against a government it does not recognise.

Follow it through. Parts come first. US export rules apply to listed items wherever they go (22 CFR 127.1), and sanctions may apply to the host. Then the host would have to accept exposure to damage claims. The rocket would pass over or near other countries' airspace. Frequencies would have to be filed through some ITU member, and a sponsor willing to do so would be accepting a share of the responsibility. Banks and insurers look for a recognised regulator, and an unrecognised government has none to show them. A sponsor state might register the launch instead, as Turkey in principle could for Northern Cyprus. That removes the question of status, because the sponsor is then the launching state, and it also moves control to the sponsor.

The attraction to the host is prestige, and a launch could serve as evidence of real government. A launch site does not give recognition, however, since recognition is a political decision made government by government. Somaliland, for example, has won limited ties through other means, including its 2020 cooperation agreement with Taiwan.

The potential is limited. The strongest version is a recognised sponsor state with a launch site on the unrecognised state's soil and a treaty between the two, with launches under the sponsor's flag. That gives the host some income and status, and it leaves the question of statehood where it was.

combo-digital-nation-satellite.essay:
Online nations have citizens, websites and sometimes constitutions, and they have no land. A satellite looks like a way to fix that. The idea is to put a small object in orbit, declare it to be the nation's territory, and point to it when anyone says the nation has no place of its own. This joins digital countries and low Earth orbit, and it has already been done once.

Asgardia is the case. A Russian engineer named Igor Ashurbeyli announced it in Paris on 12 October 2016, and people joined online, over 100,000 within two days. On 12 November 2017 an Antares rocket from Virginia launched a Cygnus cargo craft to the International Space Station, and on 6 December, after leaving the station, Cygnus released the 2.8 kilogram satellite Asgardia-1. Asgardia then described itself as the first nation with all its territory in space. The satellite burned up on 12 September 2022 and no replacement has been reported. A press release of 2025 claims over one million citizens, and no state or UN body recognises it.

The settled law on this is clear. The Montevideo Convention of 1933 sets the usual tests for statehood, and one of them is a defined territory. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 says that outer space cannot be appropriated by any country by claim, use, occupation or other means (Article II). Legal scholars argued that because US companies launched Asgardia's satellite on a NASA-funded mission, the United States was the launching state and remained responsible, and that Article VIII of the treaty kept authority over the object with the state of registry. A satellite in law is an object. It is property under some country's law, and it is no more territory than a car is.

Some points are more open than that makes them sound. Asgardia's backers reasoned that by becoming a nation they could escape the restrictions on private space activity. No rule says only existing states may become states. The ban in Article II is written to stop states and, in the widely held view, those acting through them from acquiring space, and it has not been tested against a brand new entity that claims only its own objects. Reading the text, it seems that claiming an object differs from claiming a part of space, so the Article II ban may not be the decisive obstacle. The territory test is. Whether a manufactured object can ever count as territory under Montevideo is untested. It seems unlikely, since ships and aircraft, which have the nationality of a state, are not treated as that state's territory for most purposes, and no ship is known to have gained statehood for anyone.

Here is what happens when someone tries. A digital nation buys a ride to orbit through a licensed launch broker. The launch provider's country is a launching state and handles the licensing and safety review. The US, for instance, requires a licence for launches within it (51 USC 50904) and would review the payload. The radio link needs a licence through a member of the International Telecommunication Union. The American company Swarm was fined $900,000 for putting satellites up without a licence, so the broker will insist on one. That places the object on a state's books, usually through the operator's home country, and Article VIII does the rest. The nation's members remain citizens of their home countries, pay their home taxes, and carry their home passports. A passport from a body that governments do not recognise gives no right to cross a border. A digital currency faces ordinary financial rules. So the satellite changes nothing about how any of them live.

The lifetime of the object is another limit. A small satellite in low orbit falls back to Earth within a few years, as Asgardia-1 did in under five. A nation whose territory has burned up must buy another, and its claim would then be interrupted. The operator could raise the orbit, but the cost then grows with the size.

What such a project does gain is publicity and something real to show to members. It can run experiments, run elections and raise money. Asgardia's parliament has met in Vienna, and it held a congress in Dubai in 2025. Satellites can also carry stored data and run servers. Cloud Constellation's SpaceBelt plan of 2015 to 2018 offered orbital storage as a way past national data laws, and trade reporters pointed out that data rules like Europe's follow the people whose data it is. It needed $480 million and raised far less.

The strongest version is honest about what it is, a voluntary association registered as a company or nonprofit in an ordinary country, using a satellite as a symbol and a platform. That is lawful and cheap by space standards. It has a low chance of any government treating it as more.

combo-resources-stepping-stone.essay:
Four countries have passed laws saying that a company may own what it extracts in space. A founder might try to build outward from that foothold. First comes a licence to mine, then ownership of what is mined, then a long-running base around the mine, then a claim that the people who live there have rights of their own. This combines space mining with the idea of a host state carving out a special zone. It is modelled on the way companies and mining camps have sometimes grown into governments on Earth.

The laws are real. The US Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015 says a US citizen engaged in commercial recovery of an asteroid or space resource is entitled to whatever is obtained, including to possess, own, transport, use and sell it, in accordance with US international obligations (51 USC 51303). The Act also says that the United States does not by this law assert sovereignty or ownership over any celestial body. Luxembourg passed a similar law in 2017, followed by the United Arab Emirates and Japan. The Artemis Accords, non-binding principles with 78 signatories by 28 October 2026, say that extraction does not inherently constitute national appropriation under Article II of the Outer Space Treaty (Section 10). The treaty itself says bodies in space cannot be appropriated by claim, use, occupation or any other means. So the ground is off limits, and the extracted material is claimed as property under national law.

Opinion is divided on whether this is consistent. Luxembourg's own Council of State, which advises on new laws, said it was unclear whether international law allows this. Russia objected to the US executive order of April 2020 on space resources. The Moon Agreement of 1979, with 17 parties, treats the Moon's resources as the common heritage of humankind, to be managed under an international system yet to be written, and Saudi Arabia left that treaty with effect from January 2024. A For All Moonkind article suggests the exit may reflect a wish to follow countries building a new custom through domestic mining laws. Those who take the view that mining is allowed compare it to fishing on the high seas, where the fish become yours once you catch them and the sea does not. No court has ruled on the question. It remains open whether national grants of title bind other states, and whether they would be respected in a court outside the granting state.

The steps beyond ownership are less well supported. Owning what you mine gives no right to the place where you mine it. Reading the text, it seems that the US law's own disclaimer and Article II together stop the claim at the extracted material, and that a mining camp would be protected only by its licence and by Article VIII's rule that its objects stay the owner's. Exclusive mining rights in an area are also not granted by any of these laws. The Hague Space Resources Working Group adopted its Building Blocks for an international framework on 12 November 2019, and they are not a treaty. Long use could create expectations on the ground. It is hard to convert those into anything like territory. The Völkerrechtsblog writer notes that in territorial cases, conduct by companies under national authorisation has established title for their state, and this is exactly why a government licensing a mine would want to avoid that reading. Article II bars the same outcome directly.

Here is how a real project would play out. A company incorporates in the US or Luxembourg to get the resource law. It needs an authorisation, and Luxembourg treats it as a licence under supervision, much as for a bank or fund, so the choice of a friendly country is also a choice of regulator. US citizens need launch licences anyway under 51 USC 50904. The company lands equipment and begins taking ice. Its home state must supervise it (Article VI), and the state would be responsible for what it does. It would give notice of its activities, and under the Accords it can announce a safety zone. Workers then live on site under their employment contract and their home states' laws. A camp grows. Eventually some residents want a say over how the base runs, and a mining company then becomes something like a local government, as the East India Company or a company town did on Earth, though these took place under far weaker international rules on territory.

Money would be the first real barrier. Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries were both set up to mine asteroids, ran short of money, and were sold in 2018 and 2019. The customer is unclear, since water in space has value only if a market exists in space. If one forms, it may be other governments' programmes, and the camp would then rely on them.

Bank financing works best with secure title, so the legal doubt raises the cost. A company could reduce doubt by operating only under a large state's protection, and that again trades away independence.

The potential is real as a first step toward any lasting presence, because ownership of what is mined can fund a base, and the rules on it have moved in recent years in favour of operators. The trend in national laws has been toward private rights. The strongest version has a licensed mine under an Accords signatory, a large settled workforce, and a charter from the home state giving the camp its own local government. A later generation might use that history as a basis for self-rule under some new treaty. No rule provides a path from one to the other, and any such step would be a matter of politics for that later generation.

add_sources.t: Working group hosted by IIASL adopts space resources provisions, Leiden University, Dec 2019

combo-launch-from-unclaimed-land.essay:
A very few pieces of land have no state claiming them. Bir Tawil, on the border of Egypt and Sudan, is the usual example, and Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica is another. A project might build a launch site there and argue that no country's "territory" is involved. It combines claims to unclaimed land with launching to orbit. The space treaties name a launching country partly by its territory, so land outside any territory looks at first like a gap.

The settled law starts with the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main space treaty. A country is liable if it launches or procures a launch, or if the launch takes place from its "territory or facility" (Article VII). The Liability Convention and the Registration Convention define a "launching State" in the same words. Those tests are alternatives, so losing the territory test leaves the others. Nothing in these treaties says a launch must take place from a state's territory. Private people have no way to hold land as a state, because territory in international law belongs to states. The same goes for Antarctica under the Antarctic Treaty, which covers everything south of 60 degrees South and freezes the claims made by seven countries (Article IV). It reserves the continent for peaceful purposes, and its Article I forbids military measures, including weapons tests. It allows inspections by parties of all stations and installations (Article VII). The treaty binds its members, and the claim that actions by outsiders create no rights is an interpretation.

The open question is what unclaimed land does to the launching-state tests. Nobody has launched from such a place, so none of this has been tested. Reading the text, it seems that land with no sovereign gives no state "territory", so the territory test would simply find no one. That says nothing about what the launch is for the people who ran it, and it does nothing to remove the other two tests. A second open point is Antarctica itself. The Antarctic Treaty does not mention launches to orbit, and it would be for members to decide whether a launch from Marie Byrd Land fits.

Follow it through at Bir Tawil. The land itself is not claimed, and the reason is that Egypt and Sudan each prefer a different line on the border. Getting there requires crossing one of those two countries. A rocket, its fuel and a launch crew would have to come through their ports, roads and permits. Both have every practical power to stop such a shipment on their own soil and no duty to allow it. Rocket parts are also defence items under export rules, so suppliers need licences (22 CFR 127.1). If the rocket flew, it would climb over the desert and over its neighbours' airspace, which they hold under Article 1 of the Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying. Previous private claimants to Bir Tawil have not built anything lasting, and reaching it depends on the states next to it.

Marie Byrd Land is free of neighbours, and it brings another set of problems. It lies very far from any port. Fuel, food and shelter would have to come from outside, and even Chile's government settlement on an island near the mainland has a major hospital over 1,000 kilometres away. The Madrid Protocol, an add-on to the Antarctic Treaty that protects the environment, applies in unclaimed Antarctica as well, and a launch uses fuel and leaves debris. Treaty parties could inspect the site and could press the home countries of the workers. A US citizen launching there would need a licence just as anywhere else outside the United States (51 USC 50904), since the statute does not depend on who owns the ground.

Radio is the same as anywhere. A launch needs tracking and flight-safety links, and frequencies are coordinated through the International Telecommunication Union, whose members are countries. Without one, the launch cannot lawfully use frequencies and has no protection against interference. Damage is a harder matter. A rocket stage falling on a ship would lead the injured state to look for a responsible party. If none qualifies as a launching state, the injured party may be left with a claim in national courts against the individuals.

The potential is very small. Unclaimed land might in theory remove one word from the launching-state tests, and it does not provide access, supplies or protection. The nearest real cases are the Bir Tawil claimants and the Marie Byrd claimants, none of whom has built anything. Remote launch sites that have succeeded have been run by states. Baikonur in Kazakhstan was built by the Soviet Union on its own territory and now runs under a lease from Kazakhstan. The strongest version would be a small scientific rocket from Marie Byrd Land under a treaty party's national programme, which would add nothing to the argument for sovereignty, since that party would be responsible for it.
